title: SN1, SN2, E1 or E2: how to decide
from: The decision flowchart handout, with the summary lists in lecture notes 11/10 (pages 4 and 5) and 11/12 (page 2)
goals: Classify the substrate, the reagent and the solvent before choosing a mechanism
Sort a reagent as a strong or weak base and as a good or poor nucleophile
Follow the flowchart from methyl through primary and secondary to tertiary
Predict the product of each branch, with the correct stereochemistry
Apply the flowchart's 'other issues' once the mechanism is known

sections.title: Start from the summaries: what each mechanism needs
sections.html:
The handout is titled 'Flow Chart for Substitution and Elimination Reactions', and it starts from one general picture: {{R3C-LG}} + {{Nu-}}. Before following its arrows, put the professor's summary lists in one table. Every branch of the flowchart is one of these lines being applied.

{{SN2}}{{SN1}} / {{E1}}{{E2}}
substratelow stericsstable carbocationneeds a β hydrogen that can be anti-periplanar to the LG
reagentgood Nu:poor Nu:strong base
leaving groupgood LGgood LGgood LG
solventpolar aproticpolar protic
kineticsbimolecular, concertedunimolecular, stepwisebimolecular, concerted
stereochemistryinversionracemizationanti-periplanar

Also from the notes: {{SN1}} is favored at lower temperature and {{E1}} at high temperature, from the same intermediate.

For any problem, collect four facts in this order, because that is the order the flowchart asks for them:

  1. The substrate: is the carbon with the leaving group methyl, primary, secondary or tertiary? (And is it {{sp3}}? Is it allylic or benzylic?)
  2. The reagent: strong base or weak base? Good nucleophile or poor? Bulky?
  3. The solvent: polar protic or not?
  4. The temperature, if it is given.

micro.t: First check that anything can happen
micro.h: Two quick tests before using the chart. Is there a good leaving group? If the group is OH, {{OCH3}}, {{NH2}} or F, substitution does not occur under these conditions (the 11/05 notes: ethanol with {{HS-}}, no reaction). Is the carbon {{sp3}}? A leaving group on a vinyl or aryl carbon does neither {{SN1}} nor {{SN2}} (relative rate 0). Question 2A of the past exam hides a vinyl iodide among ordinary halides to see whether you check.

macro.t: How much of the exam is this decision
macro.h: On the past exam, Questions 1B, 2A, 2B, 3A, 3C, 3D, 5A, 6A, 7A and 7B all begin with the same unstated question: which of the four mechanisms is operating? Sometimes that is the whole question (1B). More often it is the first step of an explanation or a mechanism. The handout itself ends with a caution worth keeping: 'This flow chart is meant as a guide; there will be exceptions to what is written.'

why.q: Why does the flowchart ask about the substrate before the reagent?
why.a: The substrate rules mechanisms out completely, while the reagent only chooses among those that remain. A methyl carbon can never form a carbocation and has no β hydrogen, and a tertiary carbon can never be attacked from the back. Once those limits are known, far fewer cases are left for the reagent and solvent to decide.

sections.title: Sorting the reagent: strong base, good nucleophile, or both
sections.html:
The flowchart uses phrases such as 'good Nu / weak base', 'bulky strong base' and 'weak base / poor Nu'. You need to place a reagent in the right box on sight. Basicity comes from the {{pKa}} of the conjugate acid. Nucleophilicity comes from the lecture's rate table (11/05, page 2).

boxreagentswhat they do
good Nu, weak base{{I-}}, {{Br-}}, {{HS-}}, {{RS-}}, {{N3-}}, {{-CN}}, :{{NH3}}substitution ({{SN2}}) wherever the carbon can be reached
fair Nu, weak base{{Cl-}}, {{CH3CO2-}}{{SN2}} on methyl, primary and secondary carbons
strong base, good Nu (non-bulky){{HO-}}, {{CH3O-}}, {{CH3CH2O-}}{{SN2}} on methyl and primary, {{E2}} on secondary and tertiary
strong base, poor Nu{{(CH3)3CO-}} (bulky), {{H-}} from NaH{{E2}}
weak base, poor Nu{{H2O}}, {{CH3OH}}, {{CH3CH2OH}}wait for a carbocation: {{SN1}} / {{E1}}

Two rules from the handout connect the boxes: a better nucleophile favors {{SN2}} over {{E2}}; a better base favors {{E2}} over {{SN2}}.

Read the conditions carefully. '{{NaOCH3}} in {{CH3OH}}' contains the strong base methoxide. '{{CH3OH}}' alone contains only the weak base methanol. The sodium or potassium is the signal that the anion is present.

micro.t: The pKa line that separates strong from weak
micro.h: Use the conjugate acids. Water 15.7, alcohols about 16, {{H2}} about 35: their conjugate bases are strong, and they cause {{E2}}. Acetic acid about 4, HF about 4 (lecture value), HCl −7, HBr −9, HI −10: their conjugate bases are weak and do not cause {{E2}} at ordinary temperatures. {{HS-}} sits between: the lecture's {{pKa}} for {{H2S}} is 10 (about 7 in most tables), which makes it a modest base and, with its large polarizable sulfur, an outstanding nucleophile.

micro.t: Bulk moves a reagent between boxes
micro.h: Methoxide and tert-butoxide are both strong bases. Methoxide is small and is also a good nucleophile. tert-Butoxide is too crowded to reach carbon (11/05, page 3: a poor nucleophile), so it is used when elimination is wanted. Question 1C of the past exam asks which of the two is the stronger nucleophile: methoxide. The one case where tert-butoxide does substitute is a methyl electrophile, as in Question 5A.

macro.h: Question 7A of the past exam gives 2-bromopropane with acetate and with ethoxide and asks why the amounts of substitution and elimination differ. The answer is this table. Acetate is a weak base (conjugate acid {{pKa}} 4) and a fair nucleophile, so it attacks carbon: mostly {{SN2}}. Ethoxide is a strong base (conjugate acid {{pKa}} 16), so it takes a β hydrogen: mostly {{E2}}. Full credit requires tying basicity to those {{pKa}} values.

why.q: Why is iodide a good nucleophile but a very weak base?
why.a: Basicity measures how strongly a species holds a proton at equilibrium, and iodide holds it very weakly, since HI is a very strong acid. Nucleophilicity measures how fast it attacks carbon, and iodide's large, polarizable electron cloud, loosely held by solvent, bonds to carbon quickly. The two properties measure different things.

sections.title: Branch 1, methyl: always SN2
sections.html:
The first question on the chart: Methyl? If yes, the answer is {{SN2}}, whatever the reagent. The handout gives the reasons in a note: a methyl carbocation is unstable and will never form, therefore no {{SN1}} or {{E1}}; there is no β hydrogen, therefore no {{E2}}.

So with a methyl substrate there is nothing to decide. Even a strong base cannot eliminate, because there is no neighbouring carbon to take a hydrogen from. Even a bulky nucleophile can reach the carbon, because only three small hydrogens surround it (relative {{SN2}} rate 1, against 0.033 for ethyl).

Worked case. Sodium cyclohexanolate with bromomethane in DMSO, from Question 6A of the past exam:

[[rxn:[O-]C1CCCCC1.[Na+] + CBr>DMSO>COC1CCCCC1 + [Na+].[Br-]]]
  1. Substrate: {{CH3Br}}, methyl.
  2. The chart says {{SN2}}. Check the reagent anyway: an alkoxide is a strong base, but there is no β hydrogen to remove.
  3. Solvent: DMSO, polar aprotic, which leaves the alkoxide unsolvated and very nucleophilic.
  4. Product: the alkoxide oxygen bonds to the methyl carbon, bromide leaves. Cyclohexyl methyl ether, cleanly.

The same branch explains why tert-butoxide with iodomethane gives tert-butyl methyl ether in Question 5A.

micro.t: No β hydrogen, no elimination: a test for any substrate
micro.h: The methyl note generalizes. Before worrying about {{E2}} or {{E1}}, look at each carbon attached to the carbon with the leaving group and ask whether it has a hydrogen. A methyl halide has no β carbon at all. A benzyl halide, {{C6H5CH2Br}}, has a β carbon with no hydrogen on it (the ring carbon). Neither can eliminate, so both give clean substitution even with strong bases. Choosing a partner that cannot eliminate is the main trick of planning a synthesis.

macro.t: Methyl transfer, in the flask and in the cell
macro.h: Because methyl substrates only do {{SN2}}, they are the dependable way to attach a {{CH3}} group to oxygen, nitrogen or sulfur. Question 3C of the past exam asks for the fastest {{SN2}} substrate with NaCN: methyl iodide. Cells use the same chemistry with S-adenosylmethionine, whose methyl group sits on a positively charged sulfur. Nucleophilic atoms on DNA, proteins and small molecules attack that methyl carbon in an enzyme-controlled {{SN2}} reaction.

why.q: Why can a methyl halide not undergo E2 even with a very strong base?
why.a: {{E2}} removes a hydrogen from a carbon next to the one carrying the leaving group, so that the C-H electrons can form a C=C. A methyl halide has only one carbon. There is no β carbon, no β hydrogen and no possible double bond.

sections.title: Branch 2, primary: SN2 unless the base is strong and bulky
sections.html:
Primary? The handout's note: for methyl and primary carbons, except benzylic and allylic ones, only {{E2}} and {{SN2}} are possible, because of low carbocation stability. Then three sub-branches.

Good Nu / weak base: {{SN2}}. Case: 1-bromobutane with sodium cyanide. Cyanide is a good nucleophile and a weak base, and the carbon is open.

[[rxn:CCCCBr + [Na+].[C-]#N>DMSO>CCCCC#N + [Na+].[Br-]]]

Otherwise, non-bulky strong base: {{SN2}}. Case: 1-bromobutane with {{CH3ONa}} in {{CH3OH}} at 25 °C, from Question 2A of the past exam. Methoxide is a strong base, but it is small and a good nucleophile, and a primary carbon is easy to reach. Substitution wins.

[[rxn:CCCCBr + C[O-].[Na+]>CH3OH;25 °C>CCCCOC + [Na+].[Br-]]]

Otherwise, bulky strong base: {{E2}}. Case: 1-bromobutane with potassium tert-butoxide. The base is too crowded to reach even a primary carbon, but it can reach a β hydrogen on C2.

[[rxn:CCCCBr + CC(C)(C)[O-].[K+]>(CH3)3COH>CCC=C + CC(C)(C)O + [K+].[Br-]]]

So for a primary substrate the default is {{SN2}}, and the one thing that turns it to elimination is bulk. The handout adds that increased branching on the α and β carbons favors {{E2}} over {{SN2}}: a primary halide with a crowded β carbon (isobutyl, relative {{SN2}} rate 3 × 10−3) gives more elimination with a strong base.

micro.t: Why the exception for allylic and benzylic
micro.h: The note excludes benzylic and allylic carbons because their cations are stabilized by resonance. The 11/10 notes say it directly: allyl-LG, {{SN1}} yes. So a primary allylic or benzylic substrate in a polar protic solvent with only a weak nucleophile can ionize and react by {{SN1}}. With a good nucleophile it still reacts by {{SN2}}, and quickly: allyl has a relative {{SN2}} rate of 1.3, higher than methyl. These substrates are good at both, and the reagent and solvent decide.

micro.t: Why the faster reaction in Question 2A is the one with methoxide
micro.h: Question 2A compares 1-bromobutane with {{CH3ONa}} in {{CH3OH}} against 1-bromobutane in {{CH3OH}} alone. Primary means {{SN2}} in both, and the {{SN2}} rate law is rate = k[RBr][Nu]. Methoxide, an anion, is a far better nucleophile than neutral methanol (compare {{HO-}} at 16,000 with {{H2O}} at 1 in the lecture table). A primary halide in methanol alone has no fast path: the nucleophile is poor and a primary cation will not form.

macro.t: The primary branch on the exam
macro.h: Besides Question 2A, the primary branch carries Question 6B: 1,2-diiodoethane has two primary carbons with excellent leaving groups, and a dithiolate is an excellent nucleophile and a weak base, so every step is {{SN2}}. It also stands behind the Williamson ether synthesis of Questions 5A and 6A: to make an ether, put the alkoxide on the bulky piece and make the halide methyl or primary, so that the chart lands on {{SN2}}.

why.q: Why does methoxide substitute on a primary halide while tert-butoxide eliminates?
why.a: Both are strong bases, so both could remove a β hydrogen. Methoxide is small enough to reach the back of a primary carbon, and substitution there is faster than elimination. tert-Butoxide's three methyl groups keep it from the carbon, so the only thing it can reach is a hydrogen on the outside of the molecule.

sections.title: Branch 3a, secondary in a polar protic solvent: SN1/E1 or E2
sections.html:
Secondary? This is the branch where all four mechanisms are possible, so the chart asks a second question first: polar protic solvent? The handout's reminder is that such a solvent solvates negative ions. It weakens anionic nucleophiles and it helps ionization.

If the solvent is polar protic (water, an alcohol), look at the reagent.

Weak base / poor Nu: {{E1}} / {{SN1}}. Case: one enantiomer of 2-butyl tosylate in water, from the 11/10 notes. Nothing in the flask is a strong base or a good nucleophile. The tosylate, a good leaving group, ionizes. The planar carbocation is attacked by water from either face.

[[rxn:CC[C@H](C)OS(=O)(=O)c1ccc(C)cc1 + O>>CC[C@H](C)O + CC[C@@H](C)O]]

Product: racemic 2-butanol, with some butenes from {{E1}}, more of them at high temperature.

Otherwise, strong base: {{E2}}. Case: 2-bromopropane with sodium ethoxide in ethanol, from Question 7A of the past exam. Ethoxide removes a β hydrogen faster than it can reach the hindered secondary carbon.

[[rxn:CC(C)Br + CC[O-].[Na+]>CH3CH2OH>CC=C + CCO + [Na+].[Br-]]]

Product: mostly propene, with a little ethyl isopropyl ether from {{SN2}}. It is not {{SN1}} / {{E1}}: the anionic base reacts with the halide before it can ionize.

micro.t: Why a strong base overrides the solvent
micro.h: A protic solvent encourages ionization, but ionization of a secondary halide is slow, because a secondary carbocation is only moderately stable. A bimolecular reaction with a strong base at a useful concentration is much faster. So the base consumes the halide by {{E2}} long before any carbocation forms. {{SN1}} and {{E1}} are what happens when nothing better is available. The chart puts it in one word: 'otherwise'.

micro.t: Substitution or elimination from the carbocation
micro.h: When the chart says {{E1}} / {{SN1}}, it means both, and the lecture gives the rule for the ratio: substitution is favored at lower temperature, elimination at high temperature. If the question says 'heat' or gives a high temperature, lead with the alkene. If the leaving group is on a stereocentre, the {{SN1}} product is racemic. And check whether the cation can rearrange to a more stable one before you draw any product.

macro.t: The secondary carbon is where exam questions live
macro.h: Methyl and tertiary substrates have short branches, so examiners who want you to reason choose secondary ones. Question 7A (2-bromopropane with two reagents), Question 2A (2-chloropentane and its tosylate), Question 3D (a secondary chloride on a cyclohexane with methoxide in methanol: strong base, {{E2}}) and Question 6A (bromocyclohexane with methoxide in methanol: {{E2}} competes and wins, which is why that route to the ether is the wrong one) are all on this branch.

why.q: Why does 2-butyl tosylate in water react through a carbocation, while 2-bromopropane with ethoxide in ethanol does not?
why.a: In water there is no strong base or good nucleophile, so nothing attacks the substrate and the only path is slow ionization. Ethoxide is a strong base at high concentration, and its bimolecular {{E2}} reaction is much faster than ionization of a secondary halide.

sections.title: Branch 3b, secondary without a protic solvent: SN2 or E2
sections.html:
If the solvent is not polar protic (DMSO, DMF, acetone), anions are not held by hydrogen bonds. Nucleophiles are at their most reactive, and carbocation formation gets less help. The carbocation mechanisms drop out, and the choice is between the two bimolecular ones.

Weak base / fair Nu: {{SN2}}. Case: (S)-2-chloropentane with sodium acetate in DMSO at 40 °C, from Question 2A of the past exam. Acetate is a weak base, so it does not remove a β hydrogen. In DMSO it is a good enough nucleophile to attack a secondary carbon.

[[rxn:CCC[C@H](C)Cl + CC(=O)[O-].[Na+]>DMSO;40 °C>CCC[C@@H](C)OC(C)=O + [Na+].[Cl-]]]

Product: 2-pentyl acetate with inversion, (S) to (R). The matching tosylate reacts faster, because tosylate is the better leaving group.

Otherwise, strong base: {{E2}}. Case: 2-bromopropane with potassium tert-butoxide in DMSO. A strong base meets a secondary carbon, and the result is the alkene.

[[rxn:CC(C)Br + CC(C)(C)[O-].[K+]>DMSO>CC=C + CC(C)(C)O + [K+].[Br-]]]

Notice the pattern across both halves of the secondary branch: a strong base gives {{E2}} in either kind of solvent. The solvent only matters for weak bases. It decides whether they wait for a carbocation (protic: {{SN1}} / {{E1}}) or attack directly (aprotic: {{SN2}}).

micro.t: What 'polar aprotic' does for the nucleophile
micro.h: Sodium acetate dissolved in DMSO: the oxygen of DMSO, at the δ− end of its S=O bond, surrounds {{Na+}} tightly. The acetate anion gets no such attention, because DMSO has no O-H to hydrogen-bond with it and its δ+ sulfur is buried between two methyl groups. The anion is left exposed and reactive. The same acetate in water would be wrapped in hydrogen bonds. This is line 4 of the lecture's {{SN2}} summary: polar aprotic solvent.

Sometimes the exam shows the product and you can use it as evidence. If a single enantiomer of a secondary substrate gives a single inverted product, the mechanism was {{SN2}}. If it gives a racemic mixture, it was {{SN1}}. In Question 2A the product is drawn as one inverted acetate, which confirms {{SN2}} and tells you the rate depends on leaving group, nucleophile and solvent in the ways the 11/05 lecture described.

macro.t: A reliable simplification for secondary halides
macro.h: With hydroxide or an alkoxide, a secondary halide gives mainly elimination, in any solvent. That is why Question 6A rejects bromocyclohexane with methoxide as a way to make cyclohexyl methyl ether. Good {{SN2}} yields on secondary carbons come from nucleophiles that are weak bases: acetate, azide, cyanide, thiolates, halides. This is how chemists invert a stereocentre on purpose, in a single clean step.

why.q: Why does acetate give substitution with a secondary halide when ethoxide gives elimination?
why.a: Acetate is a weak base, about 12 {{pKa}} units weaker than ethoxide, so it cannot remove a β hydrogen at a useful rate and attacks carbon instead. Ethoxide is basic enough to take the hydrogen, and for a hindered secondary carbon that is faster than backside attack.

sections.title: Branch 4, tertiary: never SN2, so E2 or SN1/E1
sections.html:
Tertiary. The handout's note: too much steric hindrance for {{SN2}}. Only one question is left.

Strong base: {{E2}}. Case: tert-butyl bromide with NaOH in water, from the 11/12 notes. The alcohol is not formed.

[[rxn:CC(C)(C)Br + [Na+].[OH-]>H2O>CC(C)=C + O + [Na+].[Br-]]]

The rate law, rate = k[t-BuBr][{{-OH}}], proves that hydroxide is in the slow step. Question 5A of the past exam is the same branch: methoxide with tert-butyl iodide gives 2-methylpropene, methanol and iodide, and no ether.

Otherwise: {{SN1}} / {{E1}}. Case: tert-butyl bromide in water alone, from the 11/10 notes. No strong base is present. The tertiary carbocation is stable enough to form, and water then either bonds to it or removes a neighbouring hydrogen.

[[rxn:CC(C)(C)Br + O>>CC(C)(C)O + CC(C)=C]]

The alcohol ({{SN1}}) is favored at lower temperature and the alkene ({{E1}}) at high temperature. Question 1B of the past exam is this branch with tert-butyl chloride: the alcohol is major, and the minor alkene forms by {{E1}} with water as the base.

Question 2B puts both tertiary branches in one problem. 2-Iodo-2-phenylpropane with NaH (strong base) goes by {{E2}}, and with water (weak base) by {{E1}}, to the same alkene.

micro.t: Tertiary gives the same alkene two ways: tell them apart on paper
micro.h: For Question 2B you must draw both mechanisms. {{E2}} with hydride: one step, three arrows (H:− to a {{CH3}} hydrogen, C-H bond to C=C, C-I bond to I), no intermediate, by-products {{H2}} and NaI. {{E1}} with water: step 1, the C-I bond breaks to give the tertiary, benzylic carbocation and iodide (slow); step 2, water takes a {{CH3}} hydrogen and the C-H pair forms the C=C, by-product {{H3O+}}. Same product, different number of steps, different rate law.

macro.t: The whole chart in four sentences
macro.h: Methyl: {{SN2}}. Primary: {{SN2}}, unless the base is strong and bulky, then {{E2}}. Secondary: strong base, {{E2}}; weak base, {{SN1}} / {{E1}} in a protic solvent and {{SN2}} in an aprotic one. Tertiary: strong base, {{E2}}; otherwise {{SN1}} / {{E1}}. If you can reproduce those four sentences and give one example of each, you can start almost every substitution or elimination question on the past exam.

why.q: Why is E2 possible at a tertiary carbon when SN2 is not?
why.a: {{SN2}} requires the reagent to reach the carbon itself, which is buried behind three alkyl groups. {{E2}} only requires it to reach a β hydrogen, and those sit on the outside of the molecule. A tertiary halide such as tert-butyl bromide has nine of them.

sections.title: After the mechanism: the flowchart's 'other issues'
sections.html:
Naming the mechanism is half the answer. The handout closes with a list of other issues that fix the exact product. Go through it every time.

issue (as on the handout)what to do
{{E2}} is anti-periplanarDraw the conformation with H and LG 180° apart. On a cyclohexane, both must be axial.
Zaitsev and Hofmann rulesMore substituted alkene with I, Br, Cl (81%, 72%, 67% in the 2-hexyl data). Less substituted with F (70%) or a bulky base.
{{SN2}} inverts a chiral centreWedge becomes dash at the attacked carbon only.
{{SN1}} racemizes (the carbocation is planar)Draw both enantiomers.
Increased branching on the α and β carbons favors {{E2}} over {{SN2}}Expect more alkene from hindered primary and from secondary substrates.
A better nucleophile favors {{SN2}} over {{E2}}; a better base favors {{E2}} over {{SN2}}Place the reagent with the {{pKa}} of its conjugate acid and the rate table.
Carbocations can rearrangeIn {{SN1}} / {{E1}}, look for a hydride, alkyl or ring-expanding shift to a more stable cation.
High temperature favors eliminationWith heat, lead with the alkene.

And the handout's last line: 'This flow chart is meant as a guide; there will be exceptions to what is written.'

micro.t: A worked case that uses three of the issues
micro.h: Question 3D of the past exam: trans-1-chloro-2-methylcyclohexane with NaOMe in MeOH. Chart: secondary, strong base, so {{E2}}. Issue 1: anti-periplanar. In the chair with Cl axial, the methyl on C2 is axial too, so the hydrogen on C2 is equatorial and cannot leave. Only C6 has an axial hydrogen. Issue 2: the Zaitsev alkene (1-methylcyclohexene) would need the C2 hydrogen, so it cannot form: geometry outranks the Zaitsev rule. Product: 3-methylcyclohexene, with the methyl stereocentre untouched.

micro.t: A checklist for the last thirty seconds
micro.h: Before leaving a question, ask: Did I show stereochemistry at the reacting carbon (inversion, or both enantiomers)? If I drew an alkene, did I choose the right β hydrogen and the right geometry? If I drew a carbocation, could it rearrange? Did I include the by-products the mechanism makes ({{Br-}}, {{H3O+}}, the conjugate acid of the base)? Does my rate law match my mechanism? Most lost points on these questions come from this list, not from choosing the wrong mechanism.

macro.t: Where each issue appears on the past exam
macro.h: Anti-periplanar: Questions 3D and 5B. Zaitsev against Hofmann: 3D and 7B. Inversion: 2A, and the list in 3A. Racemization and planarity: 3A. Better base against better nucleophile: 7A, 5A and 1C. Rearrangement: Question 9 and the 11/10 homework. Temperature: Question 1B, where the alcohol is the major product and the alkene the minor one. The next chapter takes the ideas that go one step past the lecture notes, one exam question at a time.

why.q: Why can the anti-periplanar requirement overrule the Zaitsev rule?
why.a: The Zaitsev rule compares the stability of alkenes that can actually form. If the hydrogen needed for the more substituted alkene cannot get anti to the leaving group, the transition state for that path lacks the orbital overlap it needs and is far too high in energy. The reaction then goes through the hydrogen that can line up.

summary: Collect four facts in order: the class of the carbon bearing the leaving group, the reagent (base strength, nucleophilicity, bulk), the solvent, and the temperature.
Methyl is always {{SN2}}: no carbocation can form and there is no β hydrogen.
Primary is {{SN2}} with good nucleophiles and with small strong bases, and {{E2}} only with a bulky strong base.
Secondary with a strong base is {{E2}} in any solvent.
Secondary with a weak base is {{SN1}}/{{E1}} in a polar protic solvent and {{SN2}} in a polar aprotic one.
Tertiary never does {{SN2}}: a strong base gives {{E2}}, and otherwise the carbocation forms and gives {{SN1}}/{{E1}}.
After choosing, apply the other issues: anti-periplanar geometry, Zaitsev or Hofmann, inversion or racemization, rearrangement, and heat favoring elimination.
The flowchart is a guide, and the handout says there will be exceptions.
